t: Learning Lesson 4: Working Memory is Limited
q: Today we're going to talk about something that is maybe the most amazing thing I've ever learned about how our minds work: the hackable limitations of working memory.
Here are a few things cognitive science is pretty settled on: We forget stuff that we're just encountering REALLY quickly, no matter how hard we try, and the only way to fix this is by CHUNKING.
Working Memory is like a sticky note in the brain — it holds what we're able to think about at any one time, BUT it's got limited room on it!
Psychologists have done about a bajillion studies on this, and even professional memorizers only have about four slots of working memory to work with.
So, here's the problem with chunking: the less you know about a topic, the harder it is to know how to chunk.
x: Working memory holds only about four chunks of information at a time, a limitation Stuart demonstrates experientially with a 15-second random-letter recall exercise rather than just stating as a fact.
The critical catch is that chunking ability depends on prior background knowledge: the less a student knows about a topic already, the harder it is to chunk new information about it.

t: How To Be A Better, Calmer Teacher With Visualization ualization/
q: Daily visualization will make you a calmer, more effective teacher. And it works immediately.
Visualization is nothing more than seeing yourself performing your job well. Whatever you visualize tends to happen more effortlessly.
Here you’ll see yourself following through like a referee . Picture your most challenging class or difficult student and you fulfilling your promise calmly.

It’s no different than an athlete who visualizes their competition ahead of time, and just as effective. Whatever you rehearse in your mind’s eye will be easier and more effective when it comes to pass.
I can visualize my day in about 30 seconds and a lesson in half that time. It’s a fast-motion activity that very briefly touches on highlights and key areas.

q: Who in this room feels like they are at least 1% less intelligent during sixth hour than they are during, say, third hour? That's not because your long-term memory has become damaged throughout the day — it's because your ability to concentrate has become fatigued.
As the day goes on, if we've been working hard to concentrate all day long, our attention becomes fatigued. That's true for all human beings — none of us can concentrate endlessly.
Because after years of driving, you overlearn the knowledge and skill that goes into it — and this makes the process pretty fantastically automatic.
There's a cognitive scientist in Virginia named Dan Willingham who puts it this way: Whenever we can, we will AVOID thinking. Why!? Because the concentration required by thinking is hard!
When you overlearn material, you don't have to concentrate as hard to think about it — and this makes learning a lot less of a drag.

t: How To Make Your Students Smarter
q: Many students do poorly because they believe they’re incapable.
This isn’t a new phenomenon. In the 1920s, psychologist and teacher Prescott Lecky conducted extensive research into academic success and self-image.

His conclusions have been repeated many times over, most notably by researcher Robert Rosenthal. Now called the Rosenthal effect, it proves that the expectations of the teacher have a dramatic affect on the performance of students.
Say often, “You don’t need me.” “You can do this.” “I believe in you.

Unless a student has an intellectual disability, there is no reason for them not to succeed in school. Yes, they have mountains to climb. Some have trauma and tough home lives. Yes, yes, and yes. Agreed.

If you can make the switch from believing they’re at the mercy of circumstance to smart, capable people who have the power to succeed just as they are , despite it all, their lives will be transformed in nine months.

t: Too Much Transparency Can Be a Bad Thing
q: Good leaders today are much more transparent and open than leaders of the past.

To engage team members and include them in decisions that affect them, leaders often share information about the early stages of a decision and how it is shaping up, even before a conclusion is reached.
Because people act on expectations, complete openness and transparency is a fool’s errand, ripe with dysfunction.
Too little information and leaders are accused (accurately) of being parental and excluding others from the process.
Too much information and team members will act as if a decision is already made, even though the idea may fizzle and be discarded.
Unfortunately, some valuable employees will leave in anticipation of a decision that never happens.
The idea that leaders can and should be fully transparent at all times is nonsense.
To hide or protect information until team members NEED to know is to treat people disrespectfully and like cogs in a wheel.
This is the push and pull of artful leadership and it is never easy.
x: This piece pushes back on the assumption that more transparency is always better leadership practice.

Timing, not just openness, determines whether transparency helps or hurts a team's stability.

q: Email is supremely ignorable. Lots of us ignore lots of emails just because as finite creatures we have to. There's too much coming at us. Sometimes, it just comes down to ignore emails or ignore sleep.

You're trading a 30-second "What can I do to improve my grade?" email for 10+ minutes of gradebook analysis, summarization, and advising. It's not that it's an unfair trade — it's just that it's an imbalanced one.
Instead, I like to offer a 15-minute meeting, with the following slots in order of my preference: After school, during lunch, before school.

As we find action items, I grab an index card and write them down for the student. Once we find the three most promising avenues for improving their grade, I hand them the index card and ask them if they'd like to use the rest of their time with me getting started on the work.
I've spent less effort analyzing their gradebook than I would have responding to the email, and they've gained a lot more than they would have had I emailed back a summary with advice.
